summary: An early specification of Domain Name System Security Extensions, adding digital signatures to DNS data so answers can be checked for authenticity. It incorporates feedback on RFC 2065 from early implementers and replaced that document. It was itself replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

eli5.summary: The internet's phone book can be tricked into giving wrong numbers. This adds a signature to each entry so you can tell that the answer is real.

questions: what is the dns sig record
what is the dns nxt record
subtitle: The first full design for signing DNS answers, so a resolver can tell real data from forged data.

tldr.problem: Plain DNS answers carry no proof of where they came from, so a resolver cannot tell genuine data from data that was altered or forged.
tldr.mechanism: Zones are signed with public key cryptography. New KEY, SIG and NXT resource records carry public keys, signatures over each record set, and signed proof that a name or type does not exist.
tldr.outcome: This specification replaced RFC 2065 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

today: RFC 2535 is obsoleted by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. It had been a Proposed Standard that obsoleted RFC 2065, and several later RFCs updated it before it was replaced.

sections.title: What the Extensions Provide
sections.content:
RFC 2535 defines DNS Security Extensions: additions to the Domain Name System that give security aware resolvers and applications data integrity and authentication through cryptographic digital signatures. The signatures are stored in the zone as ordinary resource records. It replaces RFC 2065 and folds in feedback from early implementers.

Three services are defined: key distribution (storing public keys in the DNS), data origin authentication and integrity (signing record sets), and optional transaction and request authentication.

The RFC is explicit about what it leaves out. DNS data is treated as public, so there are no access control lists and no confidentiality for queries or responses. Protection against denial of service is not provided either.
sections.eli5: It gives the internet's phone book three tools: a place to keep public keys, a signature on every entry, and a way to sign the whole conversation. It does not hide what you ask for.

sections.title: The KEY Record and Zone Trust
sections.content:
A KEY resource record (type 25) holds a public key for a name. That name can be a zone, a host or other end entity, or a user. The record has flags, a protocol octet, an algorithm octet and the key itself. Two flag bits can be set to the "no key" value, which lets a signed KEY record assert that a zone is not secured.

The algorithm octet names the signature scheme. Number 3, DSA, is mandatory to implement, and number 1, RSA/MD5, is recommended. Numbers 253 and 254 are for private algorithms named by a domain name or an OID.

For any algorithm a zone is treated as secure, unsecured or experimentally secure, depending on the trusted zone KEY records found for it. In a secure zone, any retrieved record that is not authenticated by a SIG is discarded as bogus. Untrusted zone KEY records MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: A KEY record is a name tag with a lock's public half attached. It can also say "this neighbourhood has no locks at all", and that statement is signed too.

sections.title: The SIG Record and Signed Answers
sections.content:
A SIG resource record (type 24) is the signature on one record set (RRset) of a given name, type and class. Its fields are the type covered, algorithm, labels, original TTL, signature expiration, signature inception, key tag, signer's name and the signature itself.

Two fields exist because DNS caches change records as they age. The original TTL is protected by the signature, while the live TTL counts down in caches and is not. A resolver bounds the TTL it uses at the original signed value. The labels field lets a resolver tell when an answer came from wildcard expansion, so it verifies against the original name. The key tag is a two octet hint that picks the right key before the costly signature check.

Signatures cover a canonical form of the data: names fully expanded and lower-cased, wildcards left as written, and the original TTL substituted. Security aware servers SHOULD send the SIG records along with the data they sign. A signature is not valid before its inception time or after its expiration time. The RFC suggests a lifetime of 4 to 16 times the TTL.

The same record type, with a type covered of zero, can sign a whole DNS reply together with the query that produced it. That transaction signature is made with the server host's key, not the zone key, and it does not by itself authenticate any record in the message.
sections.eli5: Every group of answers gets a stamp saying who signed it and when the stamp runs out. Old stamps are ignored, so an out-of-date answer cannot be passed off as fresh.

sections.title: Proving a Name or Type Does Not Exist
sections.content:
Signing the records that exist does not prove that others do not. The NXT record (type 30) fills that gap. Its owner name is an existing name in the zone, and its data holds the next name in canonical order plus a bitmap of the record types present at the owner name. Together the NXT records form a chain through every name in the zone. The last one points back to the zone name, so the name space is treated as circular.

When a security aware server answers for a name that does not exist, it returns the NXDOMAIN error with the NXT record whose interval covers the name, and its SIG, in the authority section. Further NXT records may be needed to show that no wildcard could have matched. For a missing type, the NXT bitmap shows the type is absent.

The RFC itself notes that a complete NXT chain lets a resolver list all names in a zone by walking the chain, even where zone transfers are prohibited.
sections.eli5: To prove a page is missing from a book, you show two neighbouring pages and say nothing is between them. NXT records are those signed neighbour notes.

sections.title: Resolving Securely with the AD and CD Bits
sections.content:
A resolver starts from at least one statically configured trusted public key. From there it chains alternating SIG and KEY records down the DNS tree: each signature names a signer, that signer's KEY is itself signed, and so on until the chain ends at a trusted key. The validity periods along the chain are intersected. Whether a given signer may sign for a given name is a resolver policy, and the RFC recommends specific rules.

Two header bits, taken from the previously must-be-zero Z field, signal between resolvers and servers. The AD (authentic data) bit in a response says the answer and authority data were authenticated by the server. The CD (checking disabled) bit in a query says pending, not yet authenticated data is acceptable. A resolver MUST NOT trust the AD bit unless it trusts the server and has a secure path to it or uses transaction security.

Signature times only mean something if clocks agree, so the RFC says any time synchronisation protocol used MUST be used securely.
sections.eli5: You begin with one key you already trust, then follow a chain of signed notes, each vouching for the next, until you reach the answer. If every link holds, the answer is real.

sections.title: Limits and Conformance
sections.content:
The RFC says plainly that, at most, these extensions guarantee the validity of records retrieved from the DNS. They do not stop someone from substituting an unauthorized host at a correct address or capturing packets sent to it. The older hardening against spoofing should not be abandoned, since it adds protection in case of key compromise.

Servers and resolvers each have two conformance levels, BASIC and FULL. A basic server can store and retrieve SIG, KEY and NXT records, while a full server also adds signatures, includes the records in responses automatically and handles the CD and AD bits. Primary servers for secure zones MUST be fully compliant.
sections.eli5: A signed phone book proves the number is the right one. It cannot stop a thief from standing at that address, so you still need other locks.

items.title: KEY (type 25)
items.text: Holds a public key for a zone, host or user name.

items.title: SIG (type 24)
items.text: Signs a record set and binds it to a signer and a time interval.

items.title: NXT (type 30)
items.text: Chains the names in a zone to prove what does not exist.
